title: Political Science A (Prof. Dr. Klaus Dingwerth, Prof. Dr. Adrian Rinscheid)
info: **Structure:** 12 weeks, 12 modules: 9 lectures + 3 digital learning units (DLUs): Politics, Power, Ideology, Institutions, DLU 1, Democracy, Policy Process, DLU 2, Social Movements, Business and Politics, DLU 3, Conclusion.

- **Exam:** written, **120 minutes, digital, on 4 February 2027**. It covers (a) the **preparatory readings**, (b) the **lecture contents**, (c) the **contents of the DLUs**. The reflection tasks and self-assessment questions prepare for it.
- 3 ECTS = 90 hours (≈ 5 h/week, 30 h exam preparation).
- **Challenge for the term:** which political innovation is best suited to strengthen the representation of the interests of future generations in climate politics?
- Your PDFs cover Sessions **1–3** (slides) plus the Heywood (2021) reading for Session 3. Readings for Sessions 1 and 2 are not among your PDFs.

questions.question: Compare Weber's concept of power with Arendt's. Then explain how Foucault expands the concept further.
questions.model: Weber: power is the probability that one actor within a social relationship can carry out his own will despite resistance, regardless of the basis → power as control (‘power over’), based on violence, threats, authority, shaping the environment; asymmetrical, freedom-restricting. Arendt: power is the human ability to act in concert; it belongs to a group, not an individual, and lasts as long as the group holds together → ‘power to’, symmetrical (shared goal), freedom-enabling; violence is distinct from power and can destroy but never create it; power needs legitimacy, not justification. Foucault: power is also productive/constitutive: modern subjects are products of power; disciplinary power is as important as sovereign power; power operates through discourse (material and immaterial structures).

keyPoints.text: Weber's definition (probability, will despite resistance, social relationship)
Weber = power over: asymmetrical / freedom-restricting (with bases)
Arendt: acting in concert, belongs to a group
Arendt = power to: symmetrical / freedom-enabling; power ≠ violence
Foucault: productive power, subjects as products of power / disciplinary power / discourse

questions.question: State Heywood's three features shared by all ideologies and the three key functions of ideologies. Illustrate them with ONE ideology from the lecture.
questions.model: Features: (a) an account of the existing order (world-view); (b) a model of the desired future (the good society); (c) a theory of how political change can and should be brought about. Functions: making sense of the world; investing politics with moral purpose; forging the collective. Example socialism: (a) humans are social; capitalism creates classes and inequality; (b) a community of equals where needs are met and solidarity replaces competition; (c) collective action, revolution or reform. It makes sense of inequality (class lens), gives a moral purpose (equality, solidarity) and forges a collective (the working class, unions).

keyPoints.text: Features applied correctly to one ideology
At least one function illustrated with the same ideology
